name: Wipers
label: Park Avenue
lede: Greg Sage taped punk records on a four-track in Portland and sold almost none of them for a decade. Then Kurt Cobain started telling anyone who asked that Nirvana learned everything from the Wipers.

eras.title: A window washer with a four-track
eras.text: Before punk reached Portland, Sage had cut blues-rock for a pro wrestler and taped records at home as a kid. By 1978 he had a trio, a rehearsal room and his own label, and he wanted the records as clear as window glass.

years.src: Far Out: Wipers and wrestlers · Wikipedia: Greg Sage
years.h: A Portland wrestler hires Sage to cut his blues-rock LP
years.p: Beauregarde, a Pacific Northwest tag-team champion, books teenage guitarist [[Greg Sage|275a4de2-cdc4-445b-b17a-501b0f75e460]] and bassist Dave Koupal for one afternoon of tape.
years.xp:
Sage first saw Beauregarde (born Larry Pitchford) on Portland TV in late 1969. Far Out reports the wrestler approached him at a show where Sage was filling in on guitar. The session was cut in a single afternoon in early 1970, and the LP came out in 1971 on F-Empire.

Sage told Far Out the studio engineer grabbed him by the collar and dragged him to the office to show off his framed certificates. Beauregarde stepped in: "You don't need to put your hands on my friend, you can deal with me." Sage said it was the only time he saw Beau upset with anyone. He reissued the record years later on his own Zeno label.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band) · Wikipedia: Greg Sage · Rolling Stone: Wipers' Is This Real? at 40
years.h: Sage, Henry and Koupal start a trio called the Wipers
years.p: Sage, drummer Sam Henry and bassist Dave Koupal form the band in Portland. Wikipedia says the name comes from Sage's job cleaning windows at a movie theater: he wanted his music that transparent.
years.xp: Sources disagree on the start year: Wikipedia has 1977, Rolling Stone says 1978. Either way, the trio was one of the first punk bands in the Pacific Northwest.

years.cap: Flyer for the Wipers' Nov. 4, 1978 show at the Playback Theatre, Portland, with a photo of Sage, Henry and Koupal
years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band) · Wikipedia: Greg Sage
years.h: Sage tapes Better Off Dead himself and presses it on Trap
years.p: The first Wipers single was recorded on Sage's 4-track in the band's rehearsal space and released on Trap, the label he ran himself.
years.xp: Trap grew into Portland's punk imprint, putting out singles by the Stiphnoyds, the Neo Boys and Sado Nation, and the 1979 live comp 10-29-79. Wikipedia dates the label to 1979 in Sage's biography but lists the 1978 single as a Trap release.

years.big: "I realized from that point forward that everything had to be a compromise."
q: I realized from that point forward that everything had to be a compromise.
years.src: Rolling Stone: Wipers' Is This Real? at 40 · Wikipedia: Is This Real?
years.h: Told his home tapes won't do, Sage books a real studio
years.p: Is This Real? is recorded in late 1979 at Recording Associates in Portland, with Sage producing.
years.xp:
Sage told Rolling Stone he had planned to make the album on his 4-track in the rehearsal room: "I was planning to do the album on my 4-track. I was totally good with that." Then he was told it needed a real studio.

His verdict on the people involved: "in those days, there were so many chefs trying to stir your stew." He kept the producer's chair anyway, and split the record into a Pos side and a Neg side instead of A and B.

eras.title: Heavier every time
eras.text: Two rhythm sections, three LPs in four years, and a sound that got heavier and stranger each time. Almost nobody outside the Northwest bought them, but Europe listened.

years.src: Wikipedia: Is This Real? · BrooklynVegan: 15 songs that influenced Nirvana (probably)
yt: Return of the Rat, from Is This Real?
years.h: Park Avenue releases Is This Real? with almost no promotion
years.p: The debut LP drew a small local following, and the opening riff of Return of the Rat outlasted everything around it.
years.xp:
Robert Christgau praised Sage's "hard-edged vocals" and "economical one-hook construction." AllMusic later allowed that the drums sound tinny and the songs win anyway.

BrooklynVegan points to "Potential Suicide" as the song Nirvana turned into the riff of "Breed."

years.src: Wikipedia: Alien Boy
years.h: Sage writes Alien Boy for a friend and gives it its own EP
years.p: Side B holds Image of Man, Telepathic Love and Voices in the Rain, outtakes from the Is This Real? sessions.
years.xp: Sage said the song came from his friend James "Jim Jim" Chasse, whose conversations and sense of vision fed several songs on the LP. The EP runs 8 minutes 54 seconds.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: Two Brads take over the rhythm section
years.p: Drummer Brad Naish (ex-Stiphnoyds) and bassist Brad Davidson replace the originals. Sam Henry joins the Rats and Dave Koupal moves to Ohio.
years.xp: Sam Henry went on to Napalm Beach, formed in 1982 with Chris Newman, and stayed in the Portland scene for the rest of his life.

years.src: Wikipedia: Youth of America · The Quietus: 30 Years On, The Wipers' Youth Of America Revisited
years.h: A ten-and-a-half-minute title track lands in hardcore's two-minute era
years.p: Youth of America was recorded at Wave Sound in Vancouver, Washington, and sold better in Europe than at home.
years.xp:
The title track runs 10:30 and When It's Over 6:30 on a 30-minute LP. The Quietus called the title track "a masterpiece of sustained intensity" with two garrotting guitar solos, and said the trio produced the album themselves and made it improbably refined. It also hears motorik Krautrock and goth in it.

Pitchfork later put the album at No. 102 on its list of the 200 best albums of the 1980s, and the title track at No. 173 among the songs. Melvins and Mission of Burma covered it.

years.cap: Flyer for Dead Kennedys with Wipers and E-18 at W.O.W. Hall, Eugene, Oct. 17
years.src: Wikipedia: Over the Edge (Wipers album) · Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: Over the Edge shortens the songs and gets the band on the radio
years.p: The third LP tightens up after Youth of America and brings the Wipers their first real modern-rock airplay.
years.xp:
A different take of "Romeo" had come out as a Trap single in 1982, with "No Solution" on the B-side. Hole covered the title track, and so did Red Fang and Mono Men.

J Mascis of Dinosaur Jr. has named Sage's guitar playing on this record as a foundation for his own.

years.src: Rock and Roll Globe: Greg Sage Is Living In The Land of the Lost · Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: Brain Eater folds owing Sage
years.p: Rock and Roll Globe reports the label that released Over the Edge folded without paying the band.
years.xp: Wikipedia says a label bankruptcy left Sage financially stranded and that he recorded his solo album Straight Ahead for Enigma to recover. It names Park Avenue Records; Rock and Roll Globe names Brain Eater.

eras.title: Sage builds a room called 421
eras.text: After the label wreckage, Sage took control: his own studio, his own tapes, a five-album deal with Restless. The Wipers became a trio built around Steve Plouf, and the records got heavier and more finished.

years.src: Razorcake: Interview with Greg Sage · Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: Sage records a solo album and helps Beat Happening in a fire station
years.p: Enigma releases Straight Ahead under his name and presses the live Wipers Tour 84 on vinyl. He is credited as producer on the 1985 self-titled debut by Olympia's [[Beat Happening|449e44cb-bcae-4c48-a1af-5d8df0f81456]].
years.xp: Sage plays down his part on the Beat Happening record. Asked by Razorcake, he said "I think I only helped them with a song or two, recording-wise, in an old fire station building."

years.cap: Sage at the Paradiso, Amsterdam, Sept. 17, 1986
years.src: Wikipedia: Land of the Lost (Wipers album) · Rock and Roll Globe: Greg Sage Is Living In The Land of the Lost
years.h: Restless signs the Wipers and Steve Plouf takes the drum stool
years.p: Land of the Lost is cut at Sage's own 421 Sound in Portland with [[Brad Davidson|62979f1a-3e6c-4865-b775-d176f6119628]] on bass, the first of three Restless albums made there. Let Me Know later lands on the River's Edge soundtrack (Enigma, 1987).
years.xp:
Maximum Rocknroll called the title track heavier and riffier than anything the Wipers had tried. Rock and Roll Globe says Restless gave the band a stable six-year deal for five albums, and Plouf stayed in the band 13 years.

The Spin Alternative Record Guide called it the most definitive Wipers record for sound and songwriting.

years.src: Rolling Stone: Wipers' Is This Real? at 40 · Wikipedia: Follow Blind
years.h: Sage names Follow Blind as his favorite of his own records
years.p: Rolling Stone reports it's the one he likes best. It runs 33:28, eleven songs, all his, cut at 421 Sound for Restless.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Circle
years.h: The Circle closes out the Restless run
years.p: Ten songs in 32 minutes 49 seconds, produced and recorded by Sage at 421 Sound.
years.xp:
The opener I Want a Way runs 2:35 and the title track, at 4:33, is the longest on the record.

Reviews were mixed. Trouser Press called the opener and the title track red herrings for the album's usual sound, and the Rough Guide to Rock praised the distorted guitar as invigorating.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band) · Rock and Roll Globe: Greg Sage Is Living In The Land of the Lost
yt: Greg Sage interview, VPRO radio, 29 March 1989
years.h: Sage calls it: no studio, no money, no more Wipers
years.p: A tour with drummer Travis McNabb ends the band. [[Brad Davidson|62979f1a-3e6c-4865-b775-d176f6119628]] moves to London and Sage to Phoenix.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says Sage ended the band over frustration with the music industry and the loss of his studio space. Dutch radio (VPRO) interviewed him on 29 March 1989, during the final stretch.

Rock and Roll Globe quotes his own goal for the group: "My goal was to make 15 albums in 10 years."

eras.title: Kurt keeps naming names
eras.text: With the band gone, Kurt Cobain kept saying it: in a British fanzine, in a BBC session, on a tribute box set.

q: We learnt everything from the Wipers.
years.src: Rolling Stone Australia: Return of the Rat · Rolling Stone: Wipers' Is This Real? at 40 · Rock and Roll Globe: Greg Sage Is Living In The Land of the Lost
years.h: Cobain credits the Wipers in a British fanzine
years.p: Kurt Cobain went on to say they played a mix of punk and hard rock at a time when nobody cared.
years.xp:
Cobain's other line, from the Rolling Stone feature: "They're the most innovative punk rock band that started the 'Seattle sound' like 15 years too early."

Rock and Roll Globe adds that Cobain went to Wipers shows as a kid.

years.src: Live Nirvana: 10/21/90 Maida Vale Studios · Rolling Stone Australia: Return of the Rat · Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: [[Nirvana|5b11f4ce-a62d-471e-81fc-a69a8278c7da]] cuts D-7 for John Peel at Maida Vale
years.p: The Wipers cover was recorded for Peel's BBC session and later surfaced on the Hormoaning EP and as a B-side to the UK Lithium CD single.

years.src: Rock and Roll Globe: Greg Sage Is Living In The Land of the Lost
years.h: Cobain offers Sage the whole Nevermind tour. He plays one show.
years.p: Rock and Roll Globe reports Sage politely turned down the invitation to open the entire tour and agreed to support just one Los Angeles concert.
years.xp: Cobain kept in touch. Before his death, Rock and Roll Globe says, he contacted Sage about producing a blues covers album of old Lead Belly songs in Sage's Phoenix studio.

years.src: Rolling Stone Australia: Return of the Rat · Wikipedia: Eight Songs for Greg Sage and the Wipers
years.h: Nirvana cuts Return of the Rat, a song it has never played
years.p: Cobain's reported answer when Geffen blocked D-7 for the tribute. Barrett Jones engineered it at Laundry Room Studio in West Seattle.
years.xp:
Thor Lindsay, who founded the label behind Eight Songs for Greg Sage and the Wipers, is the source for the quote. Cobain then sent the new track in on DAT.

Rolling Stone Australia relays Jones's account: the band cut Return of the Rat with Oh, the Guilt and Curmudgeon in very few takes, and "they had never even played it before."

years.src: Wikipedia: Eight Songs for Greg Sage and the Wipers · Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: Four colored 7-inches make up Eight Songs for Greg Sage and the Wipers
years.p: Tim/Kerr presses 10,000 sets with Nirvana, [[Hole|1dcc8968-f2cd-441c-beda-6270f70f2863]], [[Poison Idea|86871dd7-f50c-40bb-a298-a144775b64ae]] and Napalm Beach.
years.xp: Hole took "Over the Edge," Poison Idea "Up Front" and Napalm Beach "Potential Suicide." The expanded CD, Fourteen Songs, added [[Nation of Ulysses|ae888df0-2a19-4895-a654-e0093875d5b6]] and [[Thurston Moore|8ba48525-d922-42ee-9775-97b7b8f9712e]].

eras.title: Two men, one studio
eras.text: Sage re-formed the Wipers as a duo with Plouf, moved the operation to Phoenix and kept recording on his own terms, first for Tim/Kerr and then on his own Zeno label.

years.src: Wikipedia: Is This Real? · Wikipedia: Alien Boy
years.h: Sub Pop puts Is This Real? back in print with the Alien Boy tracks
years.p: The CD remaster adds the EP and uses the cover art from the 1987 German pressing, on Sub Pop.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: Silver Sail restarts the band as a duo
years.p: Sage and Plouf make the album for Tim/Kerr.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Herd · Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: The Herd, second Tim/Kerr album of the duo years
years.p: Twelve songs, recorded by Sage at his own Zeno Studios in Phoenix and out February 20. Return of the Rat also appears that year on the Hype! soundtrack from Sub Pop.

years.src: Rock and Roll Globe: Greg Sage Is Living In The Land of the Lost
years.h: Sage storms off the last Wipers show after a handful of songs
years.p: Rock and Roll Globe lists the July 19 New Music Seminar showcase in New York as the band's final concert, and says Sage left over incorrect amplifier specifications.

years.src: Wikipedia: Power in One · Rolling Stone: Wipers' Is This Real? at 40
years.h: Power in One ends the run on Zeno
years.p: Released October 22, the last Wipers album and the first on the label Sage founded himself.
years.xp:
Fourteen songs in 46:33, written, produced and recorded by Sage at Zeno Studios in Phoenix, with Plouf on drums.

Rolling Stone reports Sage put out nine more records after the debut and stepped away from public view after 1999.

eras.title: Everybody else catches up
eras.text: The records stayed out of print, the covers kept coming, and a documentary borrowed the title of a Wipers song. Sage kept running Zeno from Phoenix.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band) · BrooklynVegan: 15 songs that influenced Nirvana (probably)
years.h: Cloud Nothings' Dylan Baldi says he was "basically trying to be the Wipers"
years.p: [[J Mascis|82315599-2215-4c3e-a36f-87be58d06ec0]], [[Mudhoney|e675295a-1efe-4247-aa3b-53b78d0cdffc]], Hot Snakes and Metz cite them too, and Cobain's journals list the first three Wipers albums among his top 50.

years.src: Wikipedia: James Chasse · Wikipedia: Alien Boy
years.h: James Chasse dies in Portland police custody
years.p: He was the friend behind Alien Boy. The Multnomah County medical examiner ruled the death accidental, from blunt force trauma.
years.xp: Brian Lindstrom's documentary Alien Boy: The Life and Death of James Chasse premiered in Portland on February 15, 2013, and takes its name from the Wipers song.

years.src: Wikipedia: Wipers (band)
years.h: Original drummer Sam Henry dies at 65
years.p: Wikipedia gives complications of stomach cancer.
